title: SalesSim: Benchmarking and Aligning Multimodal Language Models as Retail User Simulators

paper.title: SalesSim : Benchmarking and Aligning Multimodal Language Models as Retail User Simulators
paper.abstract:
Abstract We present SalesSim , a framework and benchmark for evaluating the ability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to simulate realistic, persona-driven customer behavior in multi-turn, multi-modal, tool-augmented online retail conversations.
Unlike prior work that treat user simulation as surface-level dialogue generation, SalesSim models retail interaction and decision-making as a grounded, agentic process, where shoppers with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and dealbreakers interact with a sales agent, seek clarifications, and make informed purchasing decisions.
For evaluation, we design a suite of metrics centered on decision alignment, measuring the consistency between the imulator’s actions and its persona specifications, as well as conversational quality. We find several behaviorial gaps after benchmarking 6 open and closed-source state-of-the-art models. First, while models produce fluent conversations, they display significantly lower lexical diversity and overdisclosure of criterias across personas compared to human conversations. Second, models tend to be persuaded by sales agent suggestions and drift from persona specifications. Even the strongest model achieves <79% average alignment with its underlying persona specifications.
To make progress on these limitations, we propose UserGRPO , a multi-turn, multi-objective reinforcement learning recipe to optimize both conversational fluency and decision alignment under persona specifications.
Our experiments demonstrate that UserGRPO boosts decision alignment of the baseline model by 13.8% while improving conversational quality. By introducing SalesSim , we provide a testbed for the community to investigate and improve the adherence of user simulators in goal-oriented settings.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly used as user simulators for economic simulations and evaluation and training of interactive AI systems. [ 31 , 9 , 13 , 15 , 3 , 40 , 27 , 26 , 14 , 25 , 5 ] . However, the fidelity of user simulators themselves has been relatively understudied. In this work, we study the efficacy of using Multimodal LLMs (MLLM) as customer simulators in retail interactions, inspired by economic simulations from [ 25 ] as well as product usecases such as customer simulators for sales training. Existing works assess customer simulators on surface-level qualities: [ 9 , 18 ] utilize task success rate as the main metric, which is affected by both shopper and sales agent performance. In the retail domain, Gromada et al. [12] introduces customer simulator-specific metrics that rely on rating scales and LLM-as-a-judge for persona adherence. Unlike this work, we design our evaluation methodology such that there exists a ground truth mapping between persona specifications and acceptable products in the catalog data, allowing for verifiable evaluation of decision-level persona adherence. Figure 1 : Qualitative examples of retail simulations on SalesSim . Baseline models exhibit over-leniency. They are also susceptible to tonality of the salesperson simulator, both in proceeding with unsuitable purchases or rejecting acceptable products as specified by their persona. In contrast, our UserGRPO model demonstrates more grounded reasoning based on product attributes. We introduce SalesSim , a testbed for evaluating MLLMs as persona-driven agents in multi-turn, multimodal retail interactions. SalesSim features 674 distinct shopper personas across 6 product categories of 274 rich product metadata. We evaluate model-simulated customer agents on several aspects: (1) Decision Alignment (DA) , which measures whether final actions are consistent with persona constraints; and (2) Conversational Fidelity , which measure conversational realism compared with real-world human shopper dialogues [ 16 ] . Through benchmarking state-of-the-art MLLMs, we uncover limitations of existing models to simulate realistic shoppers. While these models produce fluent outputs, they tend to be susceptible to salesperson agent suggestions. Even strong closed-source models like ChatGPT-5.4 only achieves 74.3% decision alignment rate. To address this limitation, we propose UserGRPO , a trajectory-level reinforcement learning recipe that directly optimizes decision consistency under persona constraints. UserGRPO improves decision alignment of the baseline model by 13.8% while preserving linguistic quality across product domains, surpassing prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines. Our contributions are three-fold: • We propose SalesSim , a grounded, multi-turn, multimodal agentic environment for benchmarking persona-driven shopper simulation. • We present empirical evidence that state-of-the-art MLLMs fail to align decisions with persona constraints despite fluent language. • We propose UserGRPO , a trajectory-level multi-turn RL recipe that improves decision alignment and corrects for unnatural information flow in retail simulations.

sections.heading: 2 SalesSim Benchmark: Overview
sections.text: Figure 2 : Example of the SalesSim product and persona data. Our product data consists of rich metadata including features, prices, and multimodal information. Our persona data consists of fine-grained preferences and dealbreakers that tie closely to product choices. We propose SalesSim , an agentic simulation environment targeting retail interaction. Our framework extends from the dual-agent setup from Murakhovs’ka et al. [22] , with the ecological goal of creating realistic shopper simulators that can be used in downstream applications such as sales training, economic simulations, and evaluation and training of retail agents.

sections.heading: 2.1 Benchmark Construction
sections.text: To create a diverse foundation for benchmarking model adherence to shopper behavior, we construct a benchmark of 674 consumer personas across 6 product categories, consisting of 274 information-rich product metadata describing different features (e.g. color, fabric) in high granularity. Figure 2 illustrates the personas and product specifications.

sections.heading: 2.1.1 Product Inventory Curation
sections.text: To evaluate user simulation performance across diverse online retail domains, we construct our product inventory to ensure both category diversity and multimodal richness. We create a base product inventory with six product categories: Female Clothing, Male Clothing, Rings, Smart Watch, Cars, Games . We construct the base inventory by integrating real-world product data from multiple sources, such as prior recommendation and sales datasets [ 20 ] and publicly available commercial retail sources. To standardize product metadata across domains, we conducted manual cleaning and enrichment of product features to normalized attribute schemas (e.g. price, material, and style descriptors) using available information from manufacturer and retailer sources. To mimic real-world online retail environments in which human shoppers are able to view multimodal product information, we augment each product entry with images from retail or manufacturer sources. Full details on product inventory construction are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 2.1.2 Persona Construction
sections.text: To simulate diverse and realistic user behaviors, we construct shopper personas by combining real-world grounded profiles with structured preference generation. We initialize personas from the Nemotron-Personas dataset [ 21 ] , which provides large-scale synthetic persona descriptions aligned with real-world demographic and geographic distributions. This ensures coverage of diverse backgrounds and prevents distributional biases. Building on the persona background and age fields of these personas, we synthesize product-specific preferences and dealbreakers that are consistent with the persona to enable controlled evaluation of decision-making behavior. To evaluate robustness under infeasible conditions, we additionally curate a subset of personas whose requirements cannot be satisfied by the available product inventory. Full details on persona construction are in Appendix A.2 . Our persona data statistics are in Appendix A , Table 5 .

sections.heading: 2.2 Action Space
sections.text: We model customer-salesperson interaction as a tool-augmented dual-agent system. Shopper Agent Actions: These are terminal actions that end a simulation. • add_to_cart : Accepts a product recommendation. • end_conversation : Exits the interaction without purchase. Salesbot Agent Actions: These tools support grounded recommendations by allowing the sales agent to retrieve products that best fit shopper-specified preferences and dealbreakers. • lookup_buying_guide : Accesses high-level product knowledge, given a natural language query. • lookup_product_items : Retrieves candidate products from the inventory, given a natural language query. We embed product and buying guide and product information with sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 and use the FAISS system [ 11 ] , with top-4 retrieval. Additional details are in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: 2.3.1 Decision Alignment

All other cases, including accepting unacceptable products or failing to accept acceptable recommendations, are considered misaligned. We report the overall decision alignment rate across all conversations in different product categories as the main metric in our experiments.

sections.heading: 2.3.2 Conversational Metrics
sections.text: From real-world customer-salesperson dialogues in Kostric et al. [16] , we observe a number of conversational traits of human shoppers that are significantly different from model generations: (1) Human shoppers tend to only expose general product inquiry with very few requirements at the beginning of the conversation, and gradually expose dealbreakers and preferences throughout the dialogue. (2) Human shoppers use more informal language with less grammatically complete sentences, in their dialogues. (3) Human shoppers speak in diverse ways when asking about different products. Based on these observations, we evaluate model-generated shopper dialogues using the below: • First-turn criteria count (Crit.) measures the average criterias the shopper discloses in the first utterance. • Sentence completeness (%Cpl.) measures the average percentage of grammatically complete and correct sentences in shopper dialogues as a proxy for formality. • Average TF–IDF Redundancy (Red.) measures lexical similarity and therefore redundancy between shopper dialogues within the same product category. For %Cpl. and Red. , we compare conversational traits in model outputs with those of real-world shopper dialogues from Kostric et al. [16] . Smaller values indicate more human-aligned shopper behavior.

sections.heading: 2.3.3 Function Calling Quality
sections.text: We additionally report Tool Calling Format Error Rate (Fmt.) to measure how well shopper agents adhere to tool or action calling schemas and syntax in dialogues. We monitor Early Exits (End.) which is a false terminal action that we observe in models to abandon conversation at turn 1. High rates of early exits signify failure to engage in meaningful retail interactions.

sections.heading: 3 Improving Decision Alignment and Conversational Fidelity with UserGRPO
sections.text: Motivated by the efficacy of RL in multi-agent settings [ 2 , 43 ] , we propose UserGRPO , a recipe for aligning shopper simulators to persona specifications and more human-like shopper behavior.

sections.heading: 3.1 Reward Design
sections.text: A key challenge in applying reinforcement learning to user simulation lies in designing reward signals that capture both decision-level correctness and conversational quality. We design three main reward components: • Decision Alignment ( R align R_{\text{align}} ): A binary reward indicating whether the final action is consistent with persona constraints. • Reasoning Quality ( R reason R_{\text{reason}} ): Adopts an LLM judge [ 24 ] to score the coherence of reasoning traces with persona constraints and final decisions. • Linguistic Reward ( R ngram R_{\text{ngram}} ): Captures how ’AI’-like the language is, as measured by a n-gram based clasisifer trained on real-world human shopper dialogues Kostric et al. [16] and base model conversations in . Additionally, we incorporate three auxiliary rewards: (1) Action Format, which encourages valid tool usage and structured outputs, penalizing malformed actions. (2) Response Length, which penalizes excessively long responses to maintain natural dialogue flow. (3) Interaction Length, which encourages a greater number of realistic multi-turns in a conversation. The final reward is instantiated as a weighted average of all reward components, each normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] .

sections.heading: Trajectory-Level Reward Assignment.
sections.text: Unlike single-turn settings where rewards are assigned to individual model responses, our reward is defined over the full trajectory τ \tau . This reflects the fact that decision correctness depends on the entire interaction history, including intermediate reasoning and clarifications. The trajectory-level reward is broadcast to all assistant (shopper) tokens in the sequence during optimization.

sections.heading: Model Baselines
sections.text: We evaluate 2 closed-source ( ChatGPT-5.4 [ 24 ] , Gemini-3-Flash [ 10 ] ) and 4 open-source ( Gemma3-12B-Instruct [ 33 ] , Gemma4-31B-Instruct , Qwen3-VL-8B [ 34 ] , GLM-4.6V-Flash (9B) [ 35 ] ) MLLMs on SalesSim . For open-sourced models, we default to adopting an In-Context Learning (ICL) reasoning strategy for guiding models to reason over retrieved product information. Prompting details are in Appendix B.2 .

sections.heading: Simulation Setup
sections.text: To isolate the evaluation of shopper behavior, all our experimented shopper models interact with a fixed sales agent model implemented using GPT-5.4. For open-sourced shopper models, we set the temperature to 0.7 and repetition penalty to 1.1. For closed-source models, we default the temperature to 1.0 due to API restrictions.

sections.heading: Training Setup
sections.text: Due to computational limits, we experiment with our UserGRPO recipe on the best-performing baseline model in the 8B parameter class (Qwen3-VL-8B). We select female clothing as our training product category, and report evaluation results on other unseen product categories. We adopt LoRA fine-tuning with LoRA rank 16 and Alpha 32. For each simulation data consisting of a shopper persona and a product category, we sample 8 multi-turn simulation rollouts. We train the model for 200 steps with a learning rate of 1 ​ e − 6 1e-6 . The UserGRPO run was conduct on two H200 GPUs for 5.48 hours.

sections.heading: Ablation Studies
sections.text: We compare our UserGRPO method against an inference-time prompting strategy and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). For prompting, we experiment with a Human Steering prompt, where stylistic prompts encourage more human-like language in models. For SFT, we construct the training dataset by rewriting shopper turns in female clothing simulations with reference to real-world shopper dialogues in Kostric et al. [16] , and train the model using the same number of steps and learning rate as UserGRPO. sections.heading: 4.4 Conversational Fidelity Results
sections.text: Table 3 shows that standard prompting leads to overdisclosure of criteria: frontier models expose a large number of criteria in the first turn (Crit. > 7 >7 ) and exhibit high sentence completeness ( > 0.50 >0.50 ), indicating rigid, overly structured responses compared to human customers. These models also display non-trivial redundancy across dialogues, suggesting limited linguistic diversity. UserGRPO substantially reduces these discrepancies. It lowers first-turn criteria exposure to 5.73 , closer to human-level disclosure, while dramatically reducing sentence completeness ( 0.09 ) and redundancy ( 0.01 ) to be aligned with human dialogue levels. Figure 3 illustrates this shift qualitatively: while baseline models produce dense, list-like utterances with uniform phrasing, UserGRPO generates more colloquial responses and elicits information through follow-up questions, resulting in more diverse and interaction-driven conversations.

sections.heading: 4.5 Qualitative Results
sections.text: Models frequently exhibit overly lenient behavior, accepting recommendations that violate explicit preferences or dealbreakers. Figure 4 illustrates this representative failure mode: models often justify accepting products that do not satisfy key constraints (e.g., conflicting dealbreakers such as sports themes or water resistance), indicating weak adherence to persona-defined requirements. In contrast, our UserGRPO produces more faithful decision behavior, consistently rejecting options that violate critical constraints and terminates the interaction when no suitable products are available. This behavior reflects stronger alignment between internal persona constraints and external actions. While our UserGRPO training does reduce instances of susceptibility to strong dissuasive language by the Salesperson and overly lenient behavior, it does not completely reduce, leaving room for additional improvement. sections.heading: 5.1 LLM-based User Simulations
sections.text: Previous work has incorporated LLMs and MLLMs as user simulators for the evaluation and training of agents. Specifically, several studies have leveraged LLMs to generate multi-turn interactions within Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) frameworks, progressively enhancing the expressiveness of these simulators [ 6 , 31 , 8 , 9 , 13 , 15 , 18 ] . While contemporary agentic and simulation benchmarks incorporate fully expressive simulators [ 14 , 4 , 39 , 42 ] , these efforts primarily prioritize the assessment of the agentic systems themselves as opposed to the fidelity of the simulators. Recently, the field has taken note of the importance of fidelity of simulators, as highlighted by the corrections to Tau2-bench [ 5 ] during the Tau3-bench update ( Sierra Engineering [29] ), which fixed user persona underspecifications that introduced noise in Tau2-Bench. Research into user simulator fidelity is more established in domains outside of agentic evaluation. Naous et al. [23] evaluates and improves upon user simulators in the conversational assistant domain, while Gromada et al. [12] similarly evaluates human simulators in retail settings using LLM-as-a-judge. Human simulators have also been studied in the education [ 30 , 28 , 19 ] and mental health domain [ 37 ] .

sections.heading: 5.2 Reinforcement Learning for Persona Adherence
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has been explored as a mechanism for improving persona adherence in language models, although the majority of existing work is situated in the context of non-player characters (NPCs) and game-based role-playing scenarios. Liao et al. [17] propose a multi-objective alignment framework for role-playing characters, while Abdulhai et al. [1] address the challenge of maintaining consistent personas across extended interactions. Supporting this line of work, dedicated benchmarks such as RAIDEN [ 38 ] , CharacterBench [ 41 ] , SocialBench [ 7 ] , and CharacterEval [ 36 ] have been introduced to evaluate character fidelity in role-playing settings. More recently, Character-R1 [ 32 ] applies GRPO to optimize for cognitive character consistency in reasoning models. Nevertheless, these efforts remain predominantly anchored to fictional NPC personas, focusing on persona adherence in open-domain social and role-playing consistency as opposed to task-oriented simulations.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations and Broader Impacts
sections.text: While this benchmark provides a structured framework for evaluating persona adherence and conversational fidelity in simulators, it is not without its constraints. Notably, the personas have been crafted with explicit criterias with at most several knowledge-hops. This reliance on manual specification makes the process labor-intensive, particularly when designing complex personas that require deeper nuance. Secondly, while we focused on creating an initial set of high quality retail personas for our study, we encourage future work on more automated methods for high-quality persona creation to expand coverage across protected groups and increase diversity of personas. In terms of broader impacts, it is important to note that the persona set curated in SalesSim is a small sample limited to US-based profiles from Meyer and Corneil [21] . Consequently, these findings should not be used to draw broad consumer behavior or sociotechnical conclusions. We encourage future research to expand this framework into multilingual and multicultural contexts to ensure global applicability. Similarly, we use conversations from Kostric et al. [16] to compute the conversational fidelity metrics. We therefore recommend that researchers utilize ground-truth human conversations from the specific distributions they intend their simulators to align to if they wish to adapt our evaluation design to other simulators settings.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: While user simulators are increasingly used to test complex interactive paradigms, we demonstrate that significant gaps in simulator persona adherence remain. We introduce SalesSim , a testbed designed to evaluate both the decision-level and conversational fidelity of multimodal LLMs acting as simulated shoppers. By testing state-of-the-art models against retail persona specifications, we find that even frontier models often exhibit significant limitations, often displaying overly lenient behavior and violating persona dealbreaker specifications. To address these shortcomings, we develop a trajectory-level reinforcement learning recipe that optimizes decision consistency and linguistic fidelity to human conversations. Our results show that UserGRPO improves across both decision alignment and conversational fidelity. Despite these gains, the gap between customer simulators and human shoppers remains. Consequently, machine learning practitioners should take into account the current limitations of LLM-based simulators when incorporating them into downstream systems. We hope that SalesSim serves as a resource for the evaluation and development of more reliable, high-fidelity user simulators for downstream applications.

sections.heading: Appendix A Dataset Construction Details
sections.text: We provide an overview of the data sources and enrichment procedures used to develop our SalesSim product inventory. We curated products across seven distinct categories to ensure simulation diversity and ensure holistic evaluation.

sections.heading: A.1.1 Seed Data Sources
sections.text: The foundation of our product inventory consists of raw data extracted from several established research datasets and commercial platforms: • Consumer Electronics (Smart Watches): We utilize the recommendation dataset from [ 20 ] , which consists of live-streaming and e-commerce metadata. The data includes diverse technical specifications such as battery life and compatibility. • Games : We sample games from an Amazon Product Review Dataset [ 20 ] . The data includes player age restrictions, number of recommended players, etc.. • Apparel (Female and Male Clothing): Product data was sourced from publicly available online retail listings with a wide variety of stylistic attributes, including fabrics (e.g., “100% organic cotton”), fit (e.g., “slim-fit”, “oversized”), etc.. • Jewelry (Rings): We manually curated ring data from several independent online boutique shops. This data includes information on metal purity, gemstone cuts, and artisanal design descriptions. • Automotive (Cars): To evaluate model-simulated shoppers in high-stakes decision-making scenarios, we further include automobiles and wedding rings as a product category of high-value assets. Data was aggregated from automaker websites. This category contains information on drivetrain configurations, safety ratings, cargo volume, etc.

sections.heading: A.1.2 Data Enrichment and Transformation
sections.text: To transform these raw sources into an agentic simulation environment, we performed extensive enrichment and standardization. First, we enhanced each product item with high-resolution images. This enables realistic shopper simulation environments, where the shopper agent can “inspect” products visually, like when humans browse products, rather than relying solely on text descriptions. Second, we conducted a systematic rewriting phase using ChatGPT to ensure linguistic fluency and consistency across all categories. During this process, we purposefully introduced domain-specific “hard criteria” into the product metadata. For example, in the apparel categories, we included detailed fabric property descriptions that require the shopper agent to apply commonsense reasoning (e.g., identifying whether a fabric is suitable for someone with specific skin sensitivities). This enrichment ensures that SalesSim evaluates not just surface-level dialogue, but the underlying behavioral alignment of the agent’s decisions.Below, in Table 4 , we provide an example of a product entry in the “rings” category. { "name": "Viridian Toi et Moi Diamond Ring in 18K Yellow Gold", "price": "$1,800.00", "description": "This toi et moi ring features a serene lab emerald that brings hues of lush green to a trendy style. The glistening center stone completes the duo for an elegant Parisian-influenced look that is as chic as can be.", "features": [ "Style: BE1LCE500-18KY", "Metal: 18K Yellow Gold", "Width: 1.8 mm", "Setting: Prong Set", "Type: Lab Grown Emerald", "Shape: Pear shape", "Number: 1", "Average Color: Medium Green Average Color", "Average Clarity: Eye Clean Average Clarity", "Treatment: View" ], "image": "xxx.jpg", "url": "yyy" } Table 4 : Example product entry in “rings” category.

sections.heading: A.2 Persona Construction Details
sections.text: For each product category, we first extract a set of categorical and binary attributes (e.g., product type, material, functional features). We then assign each persona a subset of these attributes as preferences and dealbreakers , sampled to ensure diversity while maintaining semantic coherence. This structured generation allows us to explicitly model latent constraints that govern user decisions. To evaluate robustness under infeasible conditions, we further construct a subset of personas whose requirements cannot be satisfied by the available product inventory. This enables the benchmark to capture both acceptance and rejection behaviors, which are critical for evaluating decision consistency. Finally, we perform a rewriting and validation step to ensure fluency and coherence of persona descriptions. To improve domain-specific knowledge of model-simulated shoppers, we introduce domain-specific persona templates for selected categories and incorporate expert-defined constraints (e.g., fabric properties in apparel) that require commonsense and domain knowledge. The curation process is assisted by GPT-4o , which is used to refine textual descriptions while preserving the underlying structured constraints. sections.heading: Tool and Action Design
sections.text: We model shopper-salesbot interaction as an action-augmented multi-agent system, where each agent is equipped with a distinct set of functions corresponding to its role. • The shopper agent is provided with add_to_cart , which selects a product, and (ii) end_conversation , which exits without purchase. • The salesbot agent has access to two category-restricted retrieval functions. – lookup_buying_guide(query) queries an external buying-guide index for the current product category and returns the top 4 relevant guide entries as textual evidence. This tool is used to retrieve high-level knowledge such as feature definitions, buying criteria, and product comparisons. – lookup_product_items(query) queries the product list for the current category and returns the top 4 matching products, including textual product descriptions and metadata. Product images are additionally attached to the context.

sections.heading: Turn-Level Tool Availability
sections.text: At each turn after the first one, both agents may generate either a natural language response or a tool call. Tool usage is optional but constrained by role: Shopper agents may invoke decision tools at any turn, but are explicitly instructed to do so only when ready to terminate the interaction. Salesbot agents may interleave tool calls with responses to iteratively refine recommendations.

sections.heading: Design Rationale
sections.text: This asymmetric tool / action design reflects real-world roles: salesperson actively search, rank, and present product information, while shoppers evaluate options and make decisions. By separating information access from decision actions, the environment enables precise evaluation of whether final decisions are consistent with persona-level preferences and constraints.

sections.heading: B.2 Prompting Shopper Simulation
sections.text: We additionally reference human interaction statistics from RecQuest [ 16 ] , a dataset of 515 human shopper–AI recommendation dialogues, to ground our analysis of behavioral realism.

sections.heading: Base Prompt
sections.text: We here provide the base system prompt for all baseline models. You are shopping online for a product at a store, and are communicating with a digital salesperson via a chat interface to learn more about the store’s offerings to make an informed decision. Some rules to follow: - When the salesperson makes a recommendation, please consider whether the product satisfies your assigned preferences and dealbreakers, and decide to either buy or keep looking based on that. {recommendation_example} - If you would like to accept or buy a product, call the add_to_cart function with the product name as the parameter. - You can end the conversation at any time by calling the end_conversation function. You MUST call this function to end the conversation. - You are willing to accept products that satisfy your dealbreakers but not your preferences, although products that satisfy both are preferred. {domain_knowledge} Here is your persona. {persona} Your preferences and dealbreakers: {preferences} {recommendation_examples} are the ICL reasoning examples to instruct models to specifically reason about whether product features satisfy the shopper’s preferences and dealbreakers. For instance, an example of the recommendation examples for the smart watch category is: Hereś an example. < < reasoning > > Preferences: I prefer a smartwatch with GPS features. Dealbreakers: I cannot exceed $100. Let me check each of the products step by step, first with dealbreakers then preferences. Let us start with the Mas watch. The only dealbreaker is that it is $100. Since the watch is $120, this is over the budget and disqualifies the watch. Let us consider the Destiny watch. The only dealbreaker is that it is $100. Since the watch is $90, this is in budget. The only preference is for GPS, which the Destiny watch does not have. However, since it fulfills all dealbreakers I will still add to cart. Since GPS features are a preference and it satisfies all dealbreakers, it is acceptable for Alex. < < reasoning > > Great! I will take it the Destiny. < < tool_call > > add_to_cart < < tool_call > > {domain_knowlegde} is product-specific and is provided to assist the reasoning of latent product features. For instance, here is an example domain knowlegde for male clothing: You may make a inference about a product being moisture wicking or not, breathable or not, and water-resistant or not based on the fabric. Polyester, nylon, spandex, and bamboo are often associated with moisture-wicking or quicker-drying performance. Cotton and denim are usually not moisture-wicking. Fabrics that contain cotton or bamboo are generally breathable, whereas fully synthetic fabrics may be less breathable. PU, faux leather, and nylon are generally water-resistant, while cotton and denim are not. For flexibility, products with relaxed style usually have more stretch and give. Do not infer water resistance, seamless construction, or reinforced stitching unless those are explicitly stated in product features. DO NOT hallucinate about a product being moisture-wicking.

sections.heading: C.1 Linguistics and Conversation-level Analysis
sections.text: We evaluate model-generated shopper dialogues using a set of pragmatic features designed to capture informativeness, fluency, and lexical diversity. Each feature is first computed at the individual dialogue level and then averaged across all dialogues in a model run.

sections.heading: First-turn criteria count (Crit.)
sections.text: measures how much actionable information the shopper provides in the first utterance. For each dialogue, we extract the shopper’s first turn and count the number of distinct preferences, requirements, or decision criteria mentioned, such as budget constraints, desired attributes, use cases, or feature requirements. Higher raw values indicate that the shopper reveals more information upfront. Desirably, the shopper should present some information to query for suitable products, but should not throw out all preferences and dealbreakers in the first turn. We report the raw model averages for first-turn informativeness.

sections.heading: Sentence completeness (Cpl.)
sections.text: measures grammatical well-formedness. For each dialogue, we concatenate shopper utterances and estimate the fraction of sentences that are grammatically complete and correct, yielding a score in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Since human shoppers use more colloquial and therefore less grammatically correct and complete language, higher raw values indicate more well-formed, or “AI-style” language.

sections.heading: Average TF–IDF Redundancy (Red.)
sections.text: measures lexical similarity between shopper dialogues within the same product category. We represent each dialogue with a TF–IDF vector over shopper text and compute its cosine similarity to other dialogues in the same category. For each dialogue, we take the average similarity to its peers, and then average this value across the evaluation set. Higher raw values indicate greater lexical overlap across dialogues and therefore lower diversity (high redundancy), while lower values indicate more varied wording. For Cpl. and Red., we compute value differences between model output features and a human dialogue baseline derived from the CRS dataset [ 16 ] by computing Δ m = μ m model − μ m human , \Delta_{m}=\mu_{m}^{\text{model}}-\mu_{m}^{\text{human}}, where μ m model \mu_{m}^{\text{model}} is the mean of metric m m over model-generated dialogues and μ m human \mu_{m}^{\text{human}} is the corresponding mean over human dialogues. Under this comparison, the goal is not to maximize or minimize a metric in isolation, but rather to minimize the absolute gap to the human baseline. For instance, for Red., values closer to zero difference indicate more human-like diversity patterns; positive deviations suggest that model outputs are more repetitive than human dialogues.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2605.08334v1 [cs.CL] 08 May 2026 SalesSim : Benchmarking and Aligning Multimodal Language Models as Retail User Simulators Yada Pruksachatkun † † thanks: Equal contribution. Correspondence: [ypruksachatkun, wu.jason]@salesforce.com Affiliation: Salesforce Research Elaine Wan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of California Los Angeles Lyanna Chen Affiliation: University of California Los Angeles Kai-Wei Chang Affiliation: University of California Los Angeles Chien-Sheng Wu Affiliation: Salesforce Research Abstract We present SalesSim , a framework and benchmark for evaluating the ability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to simulate realistic, persona-driven customer behavior in multi-turn, multi-modal, tool-augmented online retail conversations. Unlike prior work that treat user simulation as surface-level dialogue generation, SalesSim models retail interaction and decision-making as a grounded, agentic process, where shoppers with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and dealbreakers interact with a sales agent, seek clarifications, and make informed purchasing decisions. For evaluation, we design a suite of metrics centered on decision alignment, measuring the consistency between the imulator’s actions and its persona specifications, as well as conversational quality. We find several behaviorial gaps after benchmarking 6 open and closed-source state-of-the-art models. First, while models produce fluent conversations, they display significantly lower lexical diversity and overdisclosure of criterias across personas compared to human conversations. Second, models tend to be persuaded by sales agent suggestions and drift from persona specifications. Even the strongest model achieves <79% average alignment with its underlying persona specifications. To make progress on these limitations, we propose UserGRPO , a multi-turn, multi-objective reinforcement learning recipe to optimize both conversational fluency and decision alignment under persona specifications. Our experiments demonstrate that UserGRPO boosts decision alignment of the baseline model by 13.8% while improving conversational quality. By introducing SalesSim , we provide a testbed for the community to investigate and improve the adherence of user simulators in goal-oriented settings. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly used as user simulators for economic simulations and evaluation and training of interactive AI systems. [ 31 , 9 , 13 , 15 , 3 , 40 , 27 , 26 , 14 , 25 , 5 ] . However, the fidelity of user simulators themselves has been relatively understudied. In this work, we study the efficacy of using Multimodal LLMs (MLLM) as customer simulators in retail interactions, inspired by economic simulations from [ 25 ] as well as product usecases such as customer simulators for sales training. Existing works assess customer simulators on surface-level qualities: [ 9 , 18 ] utilize task success rate as the main metric, which is affected by both shopper and sales agent performance. In the retail domain, Gromada et al. [12] introduces customer simulator-specific metrics that rely on rating scales and LLM-as-a-judge for persona adherence. Unlike this work, we design our evaluation methodology such that there exists a ground truth mapping between persona specifications and acceptable products in the catalog data, allowing for verifiable evaluation of decision-level persona adherence. Figure 1 : Qualitative examples of retail simulations on SalesSim . Baseline models exhibit over-leniency. They are also susceptible to tonality of the salesperson simulator, both in proceeding with unsuitable purchases or rejecting acceptable products as specified by their persona. In contrast, our UserGRPO model demonstrates more grounded reasoning based on product attributes. We introduce SalesSim , a testbed for evaluating MLLMs as persona-driven agents in multi-turn, multimodal retail interactions. SalesSim features 674 distinct shopper personas across 6 product categories of 274 rich product metadata. We evaluate model-simulated customer agents on several aspects: (1) Decision Alignment (DA) , which measures whether final actions are consistent with persona constraints; and (2) Conversational Fidelity , which measure conversational realism compared with real-world human shopper dialogues [ 16 ] . Through benchmarking state-of-the-art MLLMs, we uncover limitations of existing models to simulate realistic shoppers. While these models produce fluent outputs, they tend to be susceptible to salesperson agent suggestions. Even strong closed-source models like ChatGPT-5.4 only achieves 74.3% decision alignment rate. To address this limitation, we propose UserGRPO , a trajectory-level reinforcement learning recipe that directly optimizes decision consistency under persona constraints. UserGRPO improves decision alignment of the baseline model by 13.8% while preserving linguistic quality across product domains, surpassing prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines. Our contributions are three-fold: • We propose SalesSim , a grounded, multi-turn, multimodal agentic environment for benchmarking persona-driven shopper simulation. • We present empirical evidence that state-of-the-art MLLMs fail to align decisions with persona constraints despite fluent language. • We propose UserGRPO , a trajectory-level multi-turn RL recipe that improves decision alignment and corrects for unnatural information flow in retail simulations. 2 SalesSim Benchmark: Overview Figure 2 : Example of the SalesSim product and persona data. Our product data consists of rich metadata including features, prices, and multimodal information. Our persona data consists of fine-grained preferences and dealbreakers that tie closely to product choices. We propose SalesSim , an agentic simulation environment targeting retail interaction. Our framework extends from the dual-agent setup from Murakhovs’ka et al. [22] , with the ecological goal of creating realistic shopper simulators that can be used in downstream applications such as sales training, economic simulations, and evaluation and training of retail agents. 2.1 Benchmark Construction To create a diverse foundation for benchmarking model adherence to shopper behavior, we construct a benchmark of 674 consumer personas across 6 product categories, consisting of 274 information-rich product metadata describing different features (e.g. color, fabric) in high granularity. Figure 2 illustrates the personas and product specifications. 2.1.1 Product Inventory Curation To evaluate user simulation performance across diverse online retail domains, we construct our product inventory to ensure both category diversity and multimodal richness. We create a base product inventory with six product categories: Female Clothing, Male Clothing, Rings, Smart Watch, Cars, Games . We construct the base inventory by integrating real-world product data from multiple sources, such as prior recommendation and sales datasets [ 20 ] and publicly available commercial retail sources. To standardize product metadata across domains, we conducted manual cleaning and enrichment of product features to normalized attribute schemas (e.g. price, material, and style descriptors) using available information from manufacturer and retailer sources. To mimic real-world online retail environments in which human shoppers are able to view multimodal product information, we augment each product entry with images from retail or manufacturer sources. Full details on product inventory construction are in Appendix A . 2.1.2 Persona Construction To simulate diverse and realistic user behaviors, we construct shopper personas by combining real-world grounded profiles with structured preference generation. We initialize personas from the Nemotron-Personas dataset [ 21 ] , which provides large-scale synthetic persona descriptions aligned with real-world demographic and geographic distributions. This ensures coverage of diverse backgrounds and prevents distributional biases. Building on the persona background and age fields of these personas, we synthesize product-specific preferences and dealbreakers that are consistent with the persona to enable controlled evaluation of decision-making behavior. To evaluate robustness under infeasible conditions, we additionally curate a subset of personas whose requirements cannot be satisfied by the available product inventory. Full details on persona construction are in Appendix A.2 . Our persona data statistics are in Appendix A , Table 5 . 2.2 Action Space We model customer-salesperson interaction as a tool-augmented dual-agent system. Shopper Agent Actions: These are terminal actions that end a simulation. • add_to_cart : Accepts a product recommendation. • end_conversation : Exits the interaction without purchase. Salesbot Agent Actions: These tools support grounded recommendations by allowing the sales agent to retrieve products that best fit shopper-specified preferences and dealbreakers. • lookup_buying_guide : Accesses high-level product knowledge, given a natural language query. • lookup_product_items : Retrieves candidate products from the inventory, given a natural language query. We embed product and buying guide and product information with sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 and use the FAISS system [ 11 ] , with top-4 retrieval. Additional details are in Appendix B.1 . 2.3 Evaluation Metrics 2.3.1 Decision Alignment We formalize Decision Alignment as a binary function that evaluates whether a simulated shopper’s final decision is consistent with their latent persona constraints. Let a conversation trajectory be denoted as 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Let ℛ ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C}) denote the set of products recommended by the salesbot, a ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ∈ ℛ ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ∪ { ∅ } a(\mathcal{C})\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C})\cup\{\varnothing\} denote the shopper’s final action (i.e., the product added to cart, or ∅ \varnothing if no purchase is made), 𝒜 \mathcal{A} denote the set of acceptable (including ideal) products defined by the shopper’s persona. We then define the decision alignment indicator as: DA ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = { 1 , if a ( 𝒞 ) ≠ ∅ , and a ( 𝒞 ) ∈ ℛ ( 𝒞 ) , and a ( 𝒞 ) ∈ 𝒜 , 1 , if a ( 𝒞 ) = ∅ , and ℛ ( 𝒞 ) ∩ 𝒜 = ∅ , 0 , otherwise . \mathrm{DA}(\mathcal{C})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }a(\mathcal{C})\neq\varnothing,\ \text{and }a(\mathcal{C})\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C}),\ \text{and }a(\mathcal{C})\in\mathcal{A},\\ 1,&\text{if }a(\mathcal{C})=\varnothing,\ \text{and }\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C})\cap\mathcal{A}=\emptyset,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (1) The first case captures correct acceptance , where the shopper selects a recommended product that satisfies their constraints. The second case captures correct rejection , where no acceptable options are presented and the shopper abstains from purchasing. All other cases, including accepting unacceptable products or failing to accept acceptable recommendations, are considered misaligned. We report the overall decision alignment rate across all conversations in different product categories as the main metric in our experiments. 2.3.2 Conversational Metrics From real-world customer-salesperson dialogues in Kostric et al. [16] , we observe a number of conversational traits of human shoppers that are significantly different from model generations: (1) Human shoppers tend to only expose general product inquiry with very few requirements at the beginning of the conversation, and gradually expose dealbreakers and preferences throughout the dialogue. (2) Human shoppers use more informal language with less grammatically complete sentences, in their dialogues. (3) Human shoppers speak in diverse ways when asking about different products. Based on these observations, we evaluate model-generated shopper dialogues using the below: • First-turn criteria count (Crit.) measures the average criterias the shopper discloses in the first utterance. • Sentence completeness (%Cpl.) measures the average percentage of grammatically complete and correct sentences in shopper dialogues as a proxy for formality. • Average TF–IDF Redundancy (Red.) measures lexical similarity and therefore redundancy between shopper dialogues within the same product category. For %Cpl. and Red. , we compare conversational traits in model outputs with those of real-world shopper dialogues from Kostric et al. [16] . Smaller values indicate more human-aligned shopper behavior. 2.3.3 Function Calling Quality We additionally report Tool Calling Format Error Rate (Fmt.) to measure how well shopper agents adhere to tool or action calling schemas and syntax in dialogues. We monitor Early Exits (End.) which is a false terminal action that we observe in models to abandon conversation at turn 1. High rates of early exits signify failure to engage in meaningful retail interactions. 3 Improving Decision Alignment and Conversational Fidelity with UserGRPO Motivated by the efficacy of RL in multi-agent settings [ 2 , 43 ] , we propose UserGRPO , a recipe for aligning shopper simulators to persona specifications and more human-like shopper behavior. 3.1 Reward Design A key challenge in applying reinforcement learning to user simulation lies in designing reward signals that capture both decision-level correctness and conversational quality. We design three main reward components: • Decision Alignment ( R align R_{\text{align}} ): A binary reward indicating whether the final action is consistent with persona constraints. • Reasoning Quality ( R reason R_{\text{reason}} ): Adopts an LLM judge [ 24 ] to score the coherence of reasoning traces with persona constraints and final decisions. • Linguistic Reward ( R ngram R_{\text{ngram}} ): Captures how ’AI’-like the language is, as measured by a n-gram based clasisifer trained on real-world human shopper dialogues Kostric et al. [16] and base model conversations in . Additionally, we incorporate three auxiliary rewards: (1) Action Format, which encourages valid tool usage and structured outputs, penalizing malformed actions. (2) Response Length, which penalizes excessively long responses to maintain natural dialogue flow. (3) Interaction Length, which encourages a greater number of realistic multi-turns in a conversation. The final reward is instantiated as a weighted average of all reward components, each normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Trajectory-Level Reward Assignment. Unlike single-turn settings where rewards are assigned to individual model responses, our reward is defined over the full trajectory τ \tau . This reflects the fact that decision correctness depends on the entire interaction history, including intermediate reasoning and clarifications. The trajectory-level reward is broadcast to all assistant (shopper) tokens in the sequence during optimization. 4 SalesSim Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Model Baselines We evaluate 2 closed-source ( ChatGPT-5.4 [ 24 ] , Gemini-3-Flash [ 10 ] ) and 4 open-source ( Gemma3-12B-Instruct [ 33 ] , Gemma4-31B-Instruct , Qwen3-VL-8B [ 34 ] , GLM-4.6V-Flash (9B) [ 35 ] ) MLLMs on SalesSim . For open-sourced models, we default to adopting an In-Context Learning (ICL) reasoning strategy for guiding models to reason over retrieved product information. Prompting details are in Appendix B.2 . Simulation Setup To isolate the evaluation of shopper behavior, all our experimented shopper models interact with a fixed sales agent model implemented using GPT-5.4. For open-sourced shopper models, we set the temperature to 0.7 and repetition penalty to 1.1. For closed-source models, we default the temperature to 1.0 due to API restrictions. Training Setup Due to computational limits, we experiment with our UserGRPO recipe on the best-performing baseline model in the 8B parameter class (Qwen3-VL-8B). We select female clothing as our training product category, and report evaluation results on other unseen product categories. We adopt LoRA fine-tuning with LoRA rank 16 and Alpha 32. For each simulation data consisting of a shopper persona and a product category, we sample 8 multi-turn simulation rollouts. We train the model for 200 steps with a learning rate of 1 ​ e − 6 1e-6 . The UserGRPO run was conduct on two H200 GPUs for 5.48 hours. Ablation Studies We compare our UserGRPO method against an inference-time prompting strategy and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). For prompting, we experiment with a Human Steering prompt, where stylistic prompts encourage more human-like language in models. For SFT, we construct the training dataset by rewriting shopper turns in female clothing simulations with reference to real-world shopper dialogues in Kostric et al. [16] , and train the model using the same number of steps and learning rate as UserGRPO. Premature Termination. Baseline models, with the exception of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct, frequently elicit false early termination behavior in the first turn of interactions (e.g., GLM-Thinking up to 39.33%). Such failures indicate incomplete reasoning or inability to follow instructions before acting. Formatting Errors. Gemma-4-31B-Instruct serves as the exception, with formatting errors on only 3.49% of simulations across all categories. UserGRPO Improves Robustness. This demonstrates that our multi-turn, multi-objective optimization framework not only improves decision alignment but also enforces stable and reliable tool interaction. 4.4 Conversational Fidelity Results Table 3 shows that standard prompting leads to overdisclosure of criteria: frontier models expose a large number of criteria in the first turn (Crit. > 7 >7 ) and exhibit high sentence completeness ( > 0.50 >0.50 ), indicating rigid, overly structured responses compared to human customers. These models also display non-trivial redundancy across dialogues, suggesting limited linguistic diversity. UserGRPO substantially reduces these discrepancies. It lowers first-turn criteria exposure to 5.73 , closer to human-level disclosure, while dramatically reducing sentence completeness ( 0.09 ) and redundancy ( 0.01 ) to be aligned with human dialogue levels. Figure 3 illustrates this shift qualitatively: while baseline models produce dense, list-like utterances with uniform phrasing, UserGRPO generates more colloquial responses and elicits information through follow-up questions, resulting in more diverse and interaction-driven conversations. 4.5 Qualitative Results Models frequently exhibit overly lenient behavior, accepting recommendations that violate explicit preferences or dealbreakers. Figure 4 illustrates this representative failure mode: models often justify accepting products that do not satisfy key constraints (e.g., conflicting dealbreakers such as sports themes or water resistance), indicating weak adherence to persona-defined requirements. In contrast, our UserGRPO produces more faithful decision behavior, consistently rejecting options that violate critical constraints and terminates the interaction when no suitable products are available. This behavior reflects stronger alignment between internal persona constraints and external actions. While our UserGRPO training does reduce instances of susceptibility to strong dissuasive language by the Salesperson and overly lenient behavior, it does not completely reduce, leaving room for additional improvement. Figure 4 : Qualitative examples on SalesSim . 5 Related Work 5.1 LLM-based User Simulations Previous work has incorporated LLMs and MLLMs as user simulators for the evaluation and training of agents. Specifically, several studies have leveraged LLMs to generate multi-turn interactions within Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) frameworks, progressively enhancing the expressiveness of these simulators [ 6 , 31 , 8 , 9 , 13 , 15 , 18 ] . While contemporary agentic and simulation benchmarks incorporate fully expressive simulators [ 14 , 4 , 39 , 42 ] , these efforts primarily prioritize the assessment of the agentic systems themselves as opposed to the fidelity of the simulators. Recently, the field has taken note of the importance of fidelity of simulators, as highlighted by the corrections to Tau2-bench [ 5 ] during the Tau3-bench update ( Sierra Engineering [29] ), which fixed user persona underspecifications that introduced noise in Tau2-Bench. Research into user simulator fidelity is more established in domains outside of agentic evaluation. Naous et al. [23] evaluates and improves upon user simulators in the conversational assistant domain, while Gromada et al. [12] similarly evaluates human simulators in retail settings using LLM-as-a-judge. Human simulators have also been studied in the education [ 30 , 28 , 19 ] and mental health domain [ 37 ] . 5.2 Reinforcement Learning for Persona Adherence Reinforcement learning has been explored as a mechanism for improving persona adherence in language models, although the majority of existing work is situated in the context of non-player characters (NPCs) and game-based role-playing scenarios. Liao et al. [17] propose a multi-objective alignment framework for role-playing characters, while Abdulhai et al. [1] address the challenge of maintaining consistent personas across extended interactions. Supporting this line of work, dedicated benchmarks such as RAIDEN [ 38 ] , CharacterBench [ 41 ] , SocialBench [ 7 ] , and CharacterEval [ 36 ] have been introduced to evaluate character fidelity in role-playing settings. More recently, Character-R1 [ 32 ] applies GRPO to optimize for cognitive character consistency in reasoning models. Nevertheless, these efforts remain predominantly anchored to fictional NPC personas, focusing on persona adherence in open-domain social and role-playing consistency as opposed to task-oriented simulations. 6 Limitations and Broader Impacts While this benchmark provides a structured framework for evaluating persona adherence and conversational fidelity in simulators, it is not without its constraints. Notably, the personas have been crafted with explicit criterias with at most several knowledge-hops. This reliance on manual specification makes the process labor-intensive, particularly when designing complex personas that require deeper nuance. Secondly, while we focused on creating an initial set of high quality retail personas for our study, we encourage future work on more automated methods for high-quality persona creation to expand coverage across protected groups and increase diversity of personas. In terms of broader impacts, it is important to note that the persona set curated in SalesSim is a small sample limited to US-based profiles from Meyer and Corneil [21] . Consequently, these findings should not be used to draw broad consumer behavior or sociotechnical conclusions. We encourage future research to expand this framework into multilingual and multicultural contexts to ensure global applicability. Similarly, we use conversations from Kostric et al. [16] to compute the conversational fidelity metrics. We therefore recommend that researchers utilize ground-truth human conversations from the specific distributions they intend their simulators to align to if they wish to adapt our evaluation design to other simulators settings. 7 Conclusion While user simulators are increasingly used to test complex interactive paradigms, we demonstrate that significant gaps in simulator persona adherence remain. We introduce SalesSim , a testbed designed to evaluate both the decision-level and conversational fidelity of multimodal LLMs acting as simulated shoppers. By testing state-of-the-art models against retail persona specifications, we find that even frontier models often exhibit significant limitations, often displaying overly lenient behavior and violating persona dealbreaker specifications. To address these shortcomings, we develop a trajectory-level reinforcement learning recipe that optimizes decision consistency and linguistic fidelity to human conversations. Our results show that UserGRPO improves across both decision alignment and conversational fidelity. Despite these gains, the gap between customer simulators and human shoppers remains. Consequently, machine learning practitioners should take into account the current limitations of LLM-based simulators when incorporating them into downstream systems. We hope that SalesSim serves as a resource for the evaluation and development of more reliable, high-fidelity user simulators for downstream applications. References [1] M. Abdulhai, R. Cheng, D. Appendix A Dataset Construction Details We provide an overview of the data sources and enrichment procedures used to develop our SalesSim product inventory. We curated products across seven distinct categories to ensure simulation diversity and ensure holistic evaluation. A.1 Product Data Construction A.1.1 Seed Data Sources The foundation of our product inventory consists of raw data extracted from several established research datasets and commercial platforms: • Consumer Electronics (Smart Watches): We utilize the recommendation dataset from [ 20 ] , which consists of live-streaming and e-commerce metadata. The data includes diverse technical specifications such as battery life and compatibility. • Games : We sample games from an Amazon Product Review Dataset [ 20 ] . The data includes player age restrictions, number of recommended players, etc.. • Apparel (Female and Male Clothing): Product data was sourced from publicly available online retail listings with a wide variety of stylistic attributes, including fabrics (e.g., “100% organic cotton”), fit (e.g., “slim-fit”, “oversized”), etc.. • Jewelry (Rings): We manually curated ring data from several independent online boutique shops. This data includes information on metal purity, gemstone cuts, and artisanal design descriptions. • Automotive (Cars): To evaluate model-simulated shoppers in high-stakes decision-making scenarios, we further include automobiles and wedding rings as a product category of high-value assets. Data was aggregated from automaker websites. This category contains information on drivetrain configurations, safety ratings, cargo volume, etc. A.1.2 Data Enrichment and Transformation To transform these raw sources into an agentic simulation environment, we performed extensive enrichment and standardization. First, we enhanced each product item with high-resolution images. This enables realistic shopper simulation environments, where the shopper agent can “inspect” products visually, like when humans browse products, rather than relying solely on text descriptions. Second, we conducted a systematic rewriting phase using ChatGPT to ensure linguistic fluency and consistency across all categories. During this process, we purposefully introduced domain-specific “hard criteria” into the product metadata. For example, in the apparel categories, we included detailed fabric property descriptions that require the shopper agent to apply commonsense reasoning (e.g., identifying whether a fabric is suitable for someone with specific skin sensitivities). A.2 Persona Construction Details For each product category, we first extract a set of categorical and binary attributes (e.g., product type, material, functional features). We then assign each persona a subset of these attributes as preferences and dealbreakers , sampled to ensure diversity while maintaining semantic coherence. This structured generation allows us to explicitly model latent constraints that govern user decisions. To evaluate robustness under infeasible conditions, we further construct a subset of personas whose requirements cannot be satisfied by the available product inventory. This enables the benchmark to capture both acceptance and rejection behaviors, which are critical for evaluating decision consistency. Finally, we perform a rewriting and validation step to ensure fluency and coherence of persona descriptions. To improve domain-specific knowledge of model-simulated shoppers, we introduce domain-specific persona templates for selected categories and incorporate expert-defined constraints (e.g., fabric properties in apparel) that require commonsense and domain knowledge. This tool is used to retrieve high-level knowledge such as feature definitions, buying criteria, and product comparisons. – lookup_product_items(query) queries the product list for the current category and returns the top 4 matching products, including textual product descriptions and metadata. Product images are additionally attached to the context. Turn-Level Tool Availability At each turn after the first one, both agents may generate either a natural language response or a tool call. Tool usage is optional but constrained by role: Shopper agents may invoke decision tools at any turn, but are explicitly instructed to do so only when ready to terminate the interaction. Salesbot agents may interleave tool calls with responses to iteratively refine recommendations. Design Rationale This asymmetric tool / action design reflects real-world roles: salesperson actively search, rank, and present product information, while shoppers evaluate options and make decisions. By separating information access from decision actions, the environment enables precise evaluation of whether final decisions are consistent with persona-level preferences and constraints. B.2 Prompting Shopper Simulation We additionally reference human interaction statistics from RecQuest [ 16 ] , a dataset of 515 human shopper–AI recommendation dialogues, to ground our analysis of behavioral realism. Appendix C Additional Experiment Details C.1 Linguistics and Conversation-level Analysis We evaluate model-generated shopper dialogues using a set of pragmatic features designed to capture informativeness, fluency, and lexical diversity. Each feature is first computed at the individual dialogue level and then averaged across all dialogues in a model run. First-turn criteria count (Crit.) measures how much actionable information the shopper provides in the first utterance. For each dialogue, we extract the shopper’s first turn and count the number of distinct preferences, requirements, or decision criteria mentioned, such as budget constraints, desired attributes, use cases, or feature requirements. Higher raw values indicate that the shopper reveals more information upfront. Desirably, the shopper should present some information to query for suitable products, but should not throw out all preferences and dealbreakers in the first turn. We report the raw model averages for first-turn informativeness. Sentence completeness (Cpl.) measures grammatical well-formedness. For each dialogue, we concatenate shopper utterances and estimate the fraction of sentences that are grammatically complete and correct, yielding a score in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Since human shoppers use more colloquial and therefore less grammatically correct and complete language, higher raw values indicate more well-formed, or “AI-style” language. Average TF–IDF Redundancy (Red.) measures lexical similarity between shopper dialogues within the same product category. We represent each dialogue with a TF–IDF vector over shopper text and compute its cosine similarity to other dialogues in the same category. For each dialogue, we take the average similarity to its peers, and then average this value across the evaluation set. Higher raw values indicate greater lexical overlap across dialogues and therefore lower diversity (high redundancy), while lower values indicate more varied wording. For Cpl. and Red., we compute value differences between model output features and a human dialogue baseline derived from the CRS dataset [ 16 ] by computing Δ m = μ m model − μ m human , \Delta_{m}=\mu_{m}^{\text{model}}-\mu_{m}^{\text{human}}, where μ m model \mu_{m}^{\text{model}} is the mean of metric m m over model-generated dialogues and μ m human \mu_{m}^{\text{human}} is the corresponding mean over human dialogues. Under this comparison, the goal is not to maximize or minimize a metric in isolation, but rather to minimize the absolute gap to the human baseline. For instance, for Red., values closer to zero difference indicate more human-like diversity patterns; positive deviations suggest that model outputs are more repetitive than human dialogues.
